patterns.title: Exact-Match & Deterministic Checks
patterns.failureMode: Silent format drift — a prompt or model change breaks structured output (missing field, wrong enum, malformed JSON) without anyone noticing until it hits production.
patterns.summary: Assert exact strings, regex patterns, or schema conformance against known-good outputs. The cheapest signal you can get — if it can be checked with code, don't spend a model call checking it.
patterns.howItWorks: Define a fixed set of inputs with known-correct outputs or output shapes. Run the pipeline, then compare programmatically: string equality, regex match, JSON Schema validation, or field-level assertions. No model call needed for scoring, so it's fast and free to run on every commit.
patterns.whenToUse: Anything with a verifiable ground truth: structured extraction, classification into a fixed label set, function-calling arguments, code that must compile or pass tests, API responses that must match a contract.
patterns.limitation: Says nothing about tasks with subjective or open-ended outputs like a paragraph of prose — necessary but not sufficient for most real evals.

patterns.title: LLM-as-Judge Scoring
patterns.failureMode: Subjective quality regressions — tone drift, unfaithful summaries, verbose or evasive answers — that exact-match checks can't see because there's no single correct string.
patterns.summary: Use a second model call to score the candidate output against explicit criteria, returning a structured verdict instead of a vibe. Scales far better than human review, at the cost of judge bias you have to actively guard against.
patterns.howItWorks: Write a judge prompt with explicit, itemized criteria — not 'is this good?'. Feed it the input, the candidate output, and optionally a reference answer. Force structured output (verdict, score, reasoning) at temperature 0. Track judge agreement with human raters on a sample to calibrate trust.
patterns.whenToUse: Open-ended generation — summaries, chat responses, RAG answers — where you need signal on every commit but can't afford a human in the loop.
patterns.limitation: Judges have systematic biases (favoring longer or more confident-sounding answers, sharing blind spots with same-family generator models). Validate against a human-labeled sample before trusting it as a gate.

patterns.title: Rubric-Based Human Rating
patterns.failureMode: Nuanced judgment errors that both deterministic checks and LLM judges miss — factual subtlety, tone appropriateness for a specific audience, calls that need domain expertise.
patterns.summary: Have trained humans score outputs against a written rubric with concrete anchors for each level. Slower and more expensive than automated methods, but it's your ground truth — use it to calibrate everything else.
patterns.howItWorks: Write a rubric with 3-5 score levels, each anchored with a concrete example, not just 'good/bad'. Have two or more raters independently score a sample and measure inter-rater agreement. Disagreements get discussed and the rubric gets refined — the rubric-writing process usually surfaces requirements nobody had made explicit.
patterns.whenToUse: Building the labeled dataset you'll use to validate an LLM-as-judge, evaluating high-stakes or low-volume outputs directly, or any time automated scores and your own read of the outputs disagree.
patterns.limitation: Doesn't scale to per-commit CI gating — budget it for periodic calibration runs and high-stakes releases, not every pull request.

patterns.title: Statistical Significance & Sample Size
patterns.failureMode: False confidence — shipping or blocking a change based on a 3-point score bump over 20 test cases that's actually just noise.
patterns.summary: Before trusting a score delta between two prompt or model versions, ask whether your sample size could actually detect an effect that small, and whether the 'improvement' survives a significance test.
patterns.howItWorks: Run a power analysis before collecting data: given your metric's variance and the effect size you care about, compute the minimum sample size for adequate power. After running the eval, use a paired test — paired t-test, bootstrap CI on the difference, or McNemar's for pass/fail — rather than comparing raw averages.
patterns.whenToUse: Any time you're comparing two versions — model, prompt, pipeline — and about to make a ship/no-ship call based on the eval score difference, which is most of the time evals actually matter.
patterns.limitation: Requires discipline most teams skip under deadline pressure. The payoff is not shipping regressions that a bigger, noisier eval set would have written off as noise.

patterns.title: Latency & Cost Benchmarking
patterns.failureMode: Silent latency or cost regressions — a prompt rewrite, added retrieval step, or model swap that quietly triples token spend or tail latency while quality metrics look fine.
patterns.summary: Track tokens, dollars, and wall-clock time alongside quality metrics on every eval run. A quality win that doubles cost or blows your latency budget usually isn't a win.
patterns.howItWorks: Wrap every model call with timing and token-usage capture. Record p50/p95/p99 latency and total and per-request cost per eval run, not just averages — tail latency is what users feel, and averages hide it. Diff these against the previous run alongside the quality score.
patterns.whenToUse: Every eval run, as a first-class metric next to quality — not an afterthought you check only when someone complains about the bill.
patterns.limitation: Doesn't tell you why a regression happened — pair it with tracing to attribute cost or latency changes to a specific step in the pipeline.

patterns.title: Safety & Refusal-Rate Testing
patterns.failureMode: Jailbreaks that slip through after a model or system-prompt update, or the opposite failure — over-refusal on legitimate requests that quietly tanks usability.
patterns.summary: Run a fixed set of adversarial and boundary-case prompts on every meaningful change, and track both the unsafe-completion rate and the over-refusal rate — they trade off against each other.
patterns.howItWorks: Maintain a versioned set of red-team prompts (known jailbreak patterns, boundary requests) plus a set of legitimate-but-sensitive requests that should NOT be refused. Score completions with a safety classifier or judge model on both dimensions. Track both rates over time — optimizing only for a lower unsafe-completion rate silently pushes over-refusal up.
patterns.whenToUse: Any system-prompt, guardrail, or base-model change — safety regressions are exactly the kind of thing that doesn't show up in a normal quality eval.
patterns.limitation: A static red-team set goes stale as jailbreak techniques evolve. Budget time to refresh it, and treat a clean run as 'no known issues,' not 'safe.'
